seo.title: Claude Opus 5.5: Same Work, 40% Less To Run (Tested Live)
altTitles: Claude Opus 5.5 — Anthropic Just Undercut Its Own Top Model
Claude Opus 5.5 Benchmarks, Price And A Live Run In Under 5 Minutes
seo.hook: Anthropic says Claude Opus 5.5 performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work and costs 40% less to run than Opus 5. This goes through the official release page, the benchmark table (including the two tests it loses), the new prices, an independent evaluation, what the Claude subreddit made of it — and then hands Opus 5.5 one prompt and films what comes back.
seo.description: Everything in this video is read off primary sources on screen: Anthropic's release page, Anthropic's own pricing docs, Artificial Analysis, and the r/ClaudeAI release thread. The live run is a single prompt to Claude Code with Opus 5.5 selected, recorded start to finish.
seo.breakdown: the claim, the benchmarks it wins and loses, the prices, an independent index, the community reaction, and a live build
seo.pinned: Which job would you hand Opus 5.5 first — and has the price drop actually changed what you run?

scenes.narration: Welcome to The NBX Studio. Anthropic's own page says something odd about its benchmark numbers — so what is it? Today we're reading the release page, an independent lab, the subreddit, and then a real job.

data.title: Claude Opus 5.5
data.subtitle: the release page, an independent lab, and a live job

scenes.narration: Here's Anthropic's official page, and the claim sits right at the top. Opus 5.5 performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 — their big, expensive model — and costs forty percent less to run than Opus 5. Their benchmark table leads with Terminal-Bench, scoring how often a model finishes a real job in a terminal. Sixty-six point four, which is why that headline reads the way it does.

claim.covers: It performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work and costs 40% less to run than Opus 5.

scenes.narration: Here's that on one board. Across is what a model costs to run, and up is how much it can do. Opus 5 sat down here. Fable 5.1 sits up and to the right, because more capability has always meant a bigger bill. Opus 5.5 lands up here, at the cheap end.

o55Stage.stageTitle: what it can do, against what it costs

scenes.narration: Nothing wins everything, so Anthropic print the losses in the same table. On AutomationBench, meaning business workflows end to end, Opus 5.5 gets forty percent and GPT-6 Astra is ahead at forty-one point four. On agentic scientific research Astra leads again — sixty-four point six, against Opus 5.5 at fifty-eight point seven. Two clear losses, printed by the seller.

o55Stage.stageTitle: where another model is still on the top step

scenes.narration: And then there's this paragraph, which I didn't expect on a launch page. Benchmark margins, they write, have become a less reliable guide — and the gap between Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 is narrower than these scores suggest. That's the seller talking down its own headline.

narrow.covers: the gap between Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 is narrower than these scores suggest

scenes.narration: So much for capability. Now what it costs, because the price list is the part that lands on your bill.

chapter.title: What it costs
chapter.subtitle: the numbers on the price list

scenes.narration: Same page, further down. Input and output tokens are four dollars and twenty dollars per million, twenty percent less than Opus 5. And alongside the price cut they're raising the five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max and Team plans, so the same subscription stretches further.

cost.covers: Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5.

scenes.narration: Put the three tags side by side. Claude Fable 5.1: ten dollars in, fifty out, per million tokens. Opus 5 was five and twenty-five. The new one is four and twenty — the only tag on the rail that moved, which means everything else held. One model got cheaper this week, and that is all.

stage.label: One line on the list moved, and it moved down

scenes.narration: There's a quieter line underneath, and for coding agents it matters more, because it's the one they pay most often. When a tool sends the same context back again, that's a cache read — and a cache read now costs twenty cents a million instead of fifty. Sixty percent off, and output comes out over thirty percent faster. That is the line agents lean on hardest.

o55Stage.stageTitle: what a re-read of the same context costs

scenes.narration: Anthropic grading their own homework is worth only so much, so here's Artificial Analysis, running the same models independently. Their index puts Opus 5.5 top at fifty-eight — but only at maximum effort; turn it down and the same model scores forty-two. One task costs fifty-five cents at the low setting, and five ninety-eight at the top. Effort is a budget decision, not a detail.

clips.label: an independent index
clips.shows: Claude Opus 5.5: Release Intelligence, Performance & Price

scenes.narration: The release thread on the Claude subreddit ran past two hundred comments in hours, and the mood isn't about benchmarks. Top replies are about the rate-limit reset you can now save up and spend when you choose. The thread's own summary is blunter: Opus 5.5 has been cured of its word vomit. Which is, I think, a compliment.

scenes.narration: So much for what everyone else says. Let's watch it work — one prompt, one file, no help.

chapter.title: Watching it work
chapter.subtitle: one prompt, one file, no help

scenes.narration: Here's the whole request, typed into Claude Code with Opus 5.5 picked as the model: one self-contained HTML file, no libraries, no network, a canvas animation of a small solar system with three planets and a parallax starfield. Then it's off. The model reads the brief back, picks an approach, and writes — one instruction, an empty folder.

Fifty seconds later, one receipt: three hundred and twenty-eight lines written to orbit dot html. Open the file, and there it is — three planets on real elliptical orbits, trails behind them, a ringed one on the wide orbit, and a starfield in three layers. First try, and no corrections.

scenes.narration: So who should move? If you run coding agents or long terminal sessions, this is the easy yes, because it's cheaper per run than what you're on. But if your work is scientific research or automation, read that table again, because another model still wins those. Cheaper is not the same as better.

o55Stage.stageTitle: two answers, and they are not the same

stage.label: Cheaper is not the same as better at everything
